title: The same spinning dancer turns clockwise for some people and anticlockwise for others

cover.alt: The spinning dancer: a black silhouette of a woman balanced on one foot with the other leg stretched out, on a grey background above a pale reflection.
cover.credit: Nobuyuki Kayahara; video by TillermanJimW · CC BY-SA 4.0

body: The animation, made in 2003 by the Japanese web designer Nobuyuki Kayahara, is only a silhouette, so it has **no depth cues** to show which leg is in front. Your visual system has to guess, and the guess can flip on its own while nothing on screen changes. In an online survey of more than 1,600 people, about two in three first saw her turning clockwise, and later research suggests the real bias is to assume we are looking down on the dancer from above.

slides.alt: A black silhouette of a woman pirouetting on one foot with her other leg stretched out, turning round about once a second against a grey background.
slides.caption: Which way is she turning? Some viewers see her suddenly reverse, even though every turn of the animation is identical.
slides.credit: Nobuyuki Kayahara; video by TillermanJimW · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt

slides.heading: About 2 in 3 people first saw her spin clockwise
slides.note: Online survey of more than 1,600 people

left.label: Myth
left.text: The way she spins reveals whether you are ‘right-brained’ or ‘left-brained’.

right.label: Fact
right.text: It is a bistable illusion, not a personality test: what you see can flip while the picture stays the same.

slides.heading: Ways to make her switch
items: Focus on the spinning foot or the shadow
Close your eyes, picture her turning the other way
Blink rapidly until the new direction sticks

slides.heading: A switch inside the brain
slides.text: The Necker cube flips in the same way, between being seen from above and from below. In a 2014 brain-scanning study of a volunteer who could reverse the dancer at will, part of the right parietal lobe was found to be responsible for the switching.

slides.question: Why can the dancer seem to spin either way?
options: Her silhouette has no depth cues
Each eye sees a different frame
slides.explanation: Without depth cues, the same outline fits a dancer turning either way. The animation never changes; your brain’s interpretation does.
